I am not a llama, though kin we are,
in puna and highlands I roam afar.
My fiber is fine and held in esteem,
and in the Andes I’m part of the scene.

On high branches I like to stay,
with many colors on display.
I am no flower, though bright I seem,
in Peru’s jungle I brightly gleam.

I am not a whole wall, yet there I shine,
my perfect shape has stood through time.
With twelve fine corners I fit just right,
and in ancient Cusco I’m in plain sight.

With threads of history I am made,
in Andean cloth I am displayed.
I am no book, yet I can tell,
ancient cultures very well.

From dark clay I came to shine,
without paint I look refined.
On the northern coast I was born,
in vessels shaped and finely worn.

In little boxes I reside,
with saints and stories held inside.
I am no church nor grand display,
yet faith and culture in me stay.

With careful brush I came to paint,
Andean life both strong and quaint.
Farmers, festivals I portray,
in a traditional artistic way.

In hardened stone I carved each face,
ancient forms I did embrace.
I am not Inca, older still,
my temple shows enduring skill.

With masks I dance and come alive,
in festivals I always thrive.
I am no face, yet I express,
tradition through my crafted dress.

With lines so vast I marked the land,
giant figures drawn by hand.
I am not art for close-up view,
from the sky I appear to you.

In finest gold I came to shine,
crafted in ancient sacred design.
I am no jewel for simple wear,
but ritual art beyond compare.

With vivid colors I am sewn,
stories of the people shown.
From the highlands I descend,
each thread a tale I intend.

I am not a wall, yet I stand out,
in Inca stonework there’s no doubt.
With twelve sides I fit just right,
in Cusco I am in plain sight.

They called me 'The Kid' though I scored like a giant; in Mexico '70 I shone like few others. With the red-and-white I lifted the Copa América, and in Argentina '78 my free kicks were pure poetry. Who am I?

I’m not a man of flesh and bone, yet I smoke with great delight,
I carry little houses, money, and wishes shining bright.
If you place a cigarette upon my lips each Tuesday or Friday night,
I’ll make sure wealth and plenty rule your home just right.
Who am I?

I’m not a primary color, yet I paint an entire month in hue,
my procession is a moving sea where the candle bearer walks through.
I survived the earthquakes upon an old adobe wall’s embrace,
and I always reach your table with a honeyed sweet in place.
What am I?

I live inside a famous painting beside a horn and a beast,
I once cured fevers worldwide from west to east.
People confuse me with a grain cooked high in the Andes’ domain,
but I am an ancient tree bark that now scarcely grows again.
What am I?

I am a wooden box with two brightly colored doors,
inside I keep traditions, saints, shepherds, and festive folklore.
My little figures are not made of plastic nor shining metal at all,
but from handcrafted potato paste and plaster, standing proud and small.
What am I?

I have the shape of a knife, yet I do not slice your bread,
I was forged in purest gold by Chimú or Sicán kings long dead.
With me they opened skulls in ancient healing ways divine,
and now I hang as decoration in your kitchen or your dining shrine.
What am I?

I do not trot like other steeds, I move with a sideways glide,
with a handkerchief and a rider, I dance with graceful pride.
My gait is smooth and gentle, not a single drop would spill from a glass,
I am the pride of the coast with my elegant and refined pass.
What am I?

I spend my days up high, enduring February’s scorching sun and August’s misty rain.
People think that because I have horns and my tongue sticking out, I must be fierce and untamed,
but truly I am only here standing guard, keeping envy and bad spirits far away from the family.
I almost always work in pairs beside a cross,
and though they say I was born in a little village in Puno,
I end up perched on concrete and tin rooftops all across the nation.
What am I?

They dress me up with blankets, buckets, and surprises bright with cheer,
around me dance the neighbors, bands, and villagers far and near.
Taking turns with an axe, they strike me blow by blow,
and when I finally hit the ground, everyone rushes fast below.
What am I?

I was born from solidarity to help in times of need,
now I’m the party on the corner, with icy beer crates and good music indeed.
For here or to go, just pitch in with your little ticket fast,
and with my “motivos profundos” I’ll keep you dancing all night long at last.
What am I?

On some random street corner stands my little rolling shrine,
filled with secret bottles and comforting clouds that rise.
I’m no bartender, yet to warm you up I handle every glass with grace,
and with flaxseed, alfalfa, and lemon I chase your laziness away.
And honestly, I’ve rescued you from hard times more than once before,
when you’re broke and can’t afford dinner, I’m the safe bet with a couple rolls and omelets from my store.
What am I?

I’m not a party piñata, yet I hold a treasure inside,
I’m not just an ice cream, yet I’m shaped like a cone with pride.
Back in the nineties, I was the prize everyone wished to gain,
and from a magical “cloud” I used to descend like rain.
What am I?

I was born from a giant egg before the whole nation’s eyes,
I’m not green nor meant to scare, but warm-hearted by design.
Alongside my blonde-haired friend, I brightened every morning show,
and with a loud ¡Refurinfunflay! my happiness would always glow.
Who am I?

My bottle was short and chubby, my colors bright like neon light,
at every schoolyard kiosk, I was always in plain sight.
My leader was a bottle cap with cool shades and lots of style,
if you were a kid in the nineties, you surely drank me for a while.
What am I?

I wear a bow upon my head and a diaper as my pants,
with ghosts around me on TV, in spooky little chants.
To start a conversation, I always ask for my “simple thing,”
and if there’s something I dislike, “Horrible, hey!” I loudly sing.
Who am I?

I’m not a coin nor paper cash, yet at school I had great worth,
I came from a crinkly packet searching for the one of my birth.
Two tiny syllables alone would seal my fate that very day:
with a “Nola” I was treasured, with a “Yala” traded away.
What am I?

My first name is a little nickname, my last name sounds like steel,
I came shyly from the countryside to a city school unreal.
A rich and cruel little boy stole all the work I’d done,
and the great poet Vallejo wrote the story of what I’d become.
Who am I?

We’re not pop stars, nor do we wear giant costumes bright,
but without our voices, Christmas just doesn’t feel right.
Dressed in red and white, we sing in voices sweet and high,
and once our record starts to play, the panettone’s standing by.
We’re a choir of children who never seem to grow old,
and all across Peru, we’re heard through loudspeakers bold.
Who are we?

I’m not a storybook, yet my name is legend,
I’m the school trip every child is eager to claim.
In just a single day, I show you coast, jungle, and highland land,
and among sea lions and jaguars, I’ve got ancient mud ruins standing grand.
You eat your chicken sandwich sitting on my little paths with delight,
and after so much walking around, your legs ache by the end of the sight.
What am I?

My name sounds pretty terrible, almost like a crime,
but I’m the king of playground games that leaves your body tired every time.
Two players stand at either side with the ball held in their hands,
while in the middle you dodge and weave like a Spartan making stands.
If the ball strikes your body, you walk away defeated from the fight,
but if you manage to catch it, they reward you with an extra “life.”
What am I?

I’m not clothing nor a jacket, yet I dress you all through March,
covering notebook covers with a shiny plastic starch.
I make your mother grumble when you put me on the wrong way around,
that’s why nowadays I’ve got a newer version already mounted and bound.
I protect your classic Loro and your dictionary from every stain in sight,
and I drive bookstores crazy during school season’s height.
What am I?
I’m not drink or passion fruit juice, but I’m the classic from your marketing classes. What am I?
Now that you eat at expensive restaurants, when you run out of drink, you miss me. But before, even when drinking emoliente, you used to call me over for a refill. What am I?
I’m on every corner; I’m an emblem of food. And I’m always next to a pharmacy and a motel. What am I?
I take you to work when there’s no other option, but the ATU is my worst nightmare. What am I?
At your home, I’m family; but don’t let them catch me in Chincha, because I end up being a dish. What am I?

I’m not a chili pepper, yet I’m known for bringing heat,
within my barracks live a thousand stories from the street.
I’m no jungle land, yet I’ve got my very own panther’s name,
and I love soccer so much the streets became my training game.
And throw some salsa on! the people already know the tale,
I even paint the walls to honor legends who will never fail.
What am I?

Now you use me for grocery runs,
and even to pay your fare on the buses around town.
With your phone and a QR code, I solve things in a flash,
I’ve changed your life — no more worrying about carrying cash.
In fact, I’d even say I’ve made the banks rethink their game,
that’s why I’ve got a green-colored buddy trying to follow my fame.
What am I?

I’ll tell you the truth — being legal’s not really my thing,
but by adding just a little extra, I help a lot of people in a pinch.
When they reach the station and the recharge line takes way too long,
everyone feels relieved the moment they hear, “saldo, saldo!” sung.
What am I?

My kingdom is one city block, my castle is a little guard booth,
my weapon is a whistle, and my vest protects the truth.
I’m the guardian, the one who opens and closes the gate,
keeping watch on everyone while my radio helps me coordinate.
And though I’m not a policeman, I’m respected all around,
that’s why, in fact, I’ve even appeared in TV dramas renowned.
Who am I?

I’m not from another planet, though my name sounds far from human,
to cool you down in summer, I’m in every neighborhood and even sold on buses.
I’ve got family too — shaved ice is a close relative of mine,
while the sandwich stands somewhere farther down the line.
I’m not juice, yet I come with every fruit you can imagine, with milk or without alike,
I’m so tasty and refreshing that when the heat gets rough, you always come back for another bite.
What am I?

I'm not a lettuce nor a tomato,

 The rest drink, smoke, and party the whole night away,

 What kind of person are you?

I'm not a detective nor a hidden camera crew,

 they shout me out on TV with a very thrilled voice:
 'Look at this, look at this!' and the moment is their choice.
 What word am I?

From Quechua I was born and stayed in Lima without a visa,
 I'm not your relative but I warm you like a brisa.
 When someone calls you this, you've earned your place in the hood,
 the most Peruvian friendship word that no dictionary understood.
 Who am I?

I bring your plates and fill your glass on the fly,
 but in neighborhood slang I'm named after a tile nearby.
 Read me backwards and you'll see what job I do,

 What am I?

I'm not 'goodbye' nor even 'see ya later' plain,
 I'm the Lima farewell with rhyme running through my vein.
 My two key words sound the same but mean something apart,

 What phrase am I?

In Lima, I'm used to talk about a special girl,
I was born from a word written backwards and changed a little in sound.
I'm not an insult, but a familiar way to refer to her,
and if someone says "my...", they're probably talking about their partner.

My name can also be found at the market,
but here I'm not served on a plate.
I appear when you wish you could disappear,
after saying or doing something unfortunate.
What am I?

At school they call me this for the smallest kid around,
 also for the newcomer who still seems to be unsound.
 It's not an insult, but not exactly praise either,
 and if you're grown and they call you this, time to grow up, chief.
 What am I?

I come from Gamarra with a label full of lies,
 I'm sold at half the price before your very eyes.
 From the outside I look Nike, Adidas, or Lacoste,
 but after one wash I shrink and fall apart at cost.
 What am I?

I'm not a chef, but I have loyal customers.
I don't own a restaurant, yet I always find a place to sell food.
Some people look for me after a party, others when money is tight.
My food is famous for being a little risky... yet people still line up for it.
Who am I?

On the highland at night they hear me shriek 'jar-jar',
 half llama, half human, condemned to wander far.
 My sin was incest, that's why I'm cursed to roam,
 and if they hunt me with a mirror, I flee my own reflection's home.
 What being am I?

I'm the pale-skinned stranger that the people dread,
 with powders I'll put you to sleep and hang you by the head.
 I take your fat for purposes nobody comprehends,
 I'm the fear of the outsider that through the Andes extends.
 Who am I?

In the jungle at night you'll hear my whistle ring,
 thin, sharp and broken, of doom it's whispering.
 Never answer me back if you hear me drawing near,
 for whoever replies will soon be buried here.
 What am I?

I'm small and bearded, I live where the mineshafts go,
 I soften veins of gold if you win my favor's glow.
 But woe to the greedy miner, the traitor and the cheat,
 for I collect my bargains with their life, I won't retreat.
 Who am I?

I look like an ordinary man inviting you to roam,
 but look closely at my feet if you find me far from home.
 One points straight ahead, the other faces back,
 I lose you in the trees with no way to retrace your track.
 What am I?

I am the mother serpent of all waters here,
 I shelter the entire river in my depths without fear.
 No one has seen me whole and lived to tell the tale,
 the shamans invoke me but would rather turn and bail.
 What am I?

By day I hide, by night I'm a hungry witch on the prowl,
 the Andes call me Achiké and that's my growl.
 They say I suck the dreams from innocent sleeping children,
 the grandparents of the Andes use me to teach lessons hidden.
 Who am I?

Shamans ride me to communicate with the spirit realm,
 they drink me in the jungle in a rite that overwhelms.
 I'm the sacred purge of the deepest Amazon,
 and my vision transforms you though your body carries on.
 What am I?

I'm the devil himself dressed in a hat and fine attire,
 I dance in the festivals of Cerro de Pasco with fire.
 Miners fear me and at the same time hold me in reverence,
 at Corpus Christi my dancers make my presence.
 Who am I?

At night I roam the streets of every town,
 looking for little kids who won't settle down.
 If you don't fall asleep when mama gives the order,
 I'll come and take you away that's my only border.
 Who am I?

A yellow shawl, black glasses, those two alone are enough to identify him. He wrote dialogues for the screen and captured power on the stage. Who is he?

Everyone calls me by that name. But it is not the name my parents gave me. The word itself means "the great one" or "the elder." Just as Avvaiyar is a title, so am I. My real name is E.V. Ramasamy. What do they call me?

I began in 1925. Before parties, before elections, before the legislative assembly, as a people's movement. I opposed caste, I opposed Brahmin dominance, I opposed blind superstition. I said a person must have dignity for themselves first. The roots of Tamil politics were planted here. What movement is this?

I am a colour. Not for fashion, but for protest. In Periyar's time this colour was given political meaning to oppose caste dominance. Later, any movement uses this colour to declare opposition. The bitterness of Tamil politics lives in me. What colour am I?

A rising sun, light that never sets. The symbol of Tamil political awakening. I appear on the party flag and on the election symbol. When I rise, darkness ends and a new day begins, that is the message. Whose symbol is this?

I served as Chief Minister for only two years. A very short tenure. But my name shaped an entire generation. They call me by a family word, "Anna," meaning elder brother. I was the first non-Congress Chief Minister in India. Who am I?

In 1971, a film actor went on a fast for political reasons. Political demand and physical suffering met in one act. This was not just a protest, it became an event that lives in people's memory. Later he became Chief Minister. Who is he?

I am a beach. But not just any beach. Tamil political leaders do not leave me even in death. Anna, MGR, Kamaraj, Jayalalithaa, Karunanidhi, all their memorials are here. No other beach in the world has so many leaders resting on it. Who am I?

No other state in India has this much. When the Supreme Court tried to cut it, we hid it inside a specific schedule of the constitution, the Ninth Schedule. That is why it survives today. What is the number that has become the symbol of Tamil Nadu's social justice?

An atheist took a line about one god as the slogan of his movement. The line, "One race, one god", was not his. A Siddhar wrote it centuries before him. But he turned it into a battle cry against caste. Whose line is it, and who repurposed it?

It was first excavated after 2015 along the Vaigai river. Before this, the Sangam age was believed to start at 300 BCE. But the carbon dating from this site pushed it back to 600 BCE. It proved that Tamil civilization was contemporary with the Indus valley. What place is this?

She was the commander of Queen Velu Nachiyar's army. The British arsenal was inside a fort where only women were allowed on one day, Vijayadasami. She poured ghee all over her body, set herself on fire, and jumped into the arsenal. She entered history as the world's first recorded suicide bomber. Who was she?

She was the first queen in India to fight against the British. Eighty years before Rani Lakshmi Bai of Jhansi. After her husband was killed, she escaped with her daughter, formed an army of women with the help of Hyder Ali. In Tamil she is called Veeramangai, the brave woman. Who is she?

In 1025 CE, a Tamil king sent his navy across the sea. His fleet reached what is today Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand. He captured a city called Kadaram and earned the title Kadaram Kondan — Conqueror of Kadaram. The only major Indian naval expedition across the open ocean in recorded history. Who was he?

In the 2nd century CE, a dam was built across the Kaveri river. Two thousand years later, it is still in use. One of the oldest still-functioning dams in the world. Who built it, and what is it called?

A temple. Its tower stands 216 feet tall. Built and consecrated in 1010 CE in just five years. The single stone at the top weighs 80 tons, one piece. According to a popular saying, at noon its shadow does not fall on the ground. Who built it?

In 1799, a South Indian chieftain was hanged. He had refused to pay taxes to the British and fought from his fort at Panchalankurichi. His famous line, "Whether it rains or the sun beats down, I shall live on my own land, and I shall not pay tax to the British." Fifty-eight years before the 1857 revolt. Who was he?

In 1965, self-immolations took place in Tamil Nadu. To protest the imposition of one language. Students came to the streets. Some set themselves on fire and died. The result was that the central government kept English as an official language. This protest preserved Tamil's distinct identity. By what name is it known?

January 14, 1969 - Pongal day. On that day, this state renamed itself. Earlier it was called Madras State. But Tamils did not like that colonial name. A victory of the Tamil pride movement. What new name was given?

A site excavated in southern Tamil Nadu. Iron age remains. Dated back to 905 BCE. Inside earthen urns - bones, jewellery, weapons. People cremated their dead and buried the bones in pots. Proof that Tamil civilization is far older than once believed. What place is this?

Ancient Tamil literature divided Tamil land into five regions, each with its own god, flower, and emotion. Mountain, forest, paddy-field, seashore, desert - what are these five regions collectively called?

One of the five tinais, the land of the mountain region. Murugan is its guardian deity, and the emotion of "lovers meeting for the first time" is its central theme. This land bears the name of a blue flower that blooms only once every 12 years. Which tinai is this?

One of the five tinais, the coastal land. Varunan is its guardian deity. Its theme is the fisherwoman waiting by the sea, watching for her departed lover's return. Its flower is not the lotus but another, a white bloom of the waters. Which tinai is this?

Among the five tinais, this one is different, it's not a separate land. It is the land that emerges when Mullai or Kurinji dries up in summer. Korravai is its goddess, and separation is its emotion. It is the path lovers walk when leaving home. Which tinai is this?

I am the only river in Tamil Nadu that flows all year round. I am born in the Pothigai hills, the sacred mountain where Agastya resides. In old Tamil poems I am called Porunai. My water has a distinct quality because of the copper in it. Who am I?

I wrap around a city like a garland. The prosperity of the Pandya capital lies in my hands. In old Tamil literature I am called Kritamaala. But I do not flow to the open sea, I end near the Palk Strait. Who am I?

I was once a royal port, but half of me lies hidden under the sea. They sang of me in Silappatikaram. Kovalan and Kannagi lived here. The sea has kept part of my body hidden, I am remembered in poetry but buried under water and sand. Who am I?

I was a Pandya port. But my wealth came not from grain or gold. The small jewels hidden inside the sea's shells were my wealth. I was one of the great pearl-fishing centers of the ancient world. Who am I?

I was a town. A railway ended at my doorstep. In 1964 a great cyclone came, in a single night it destroyed me. Train, temple, people, all swept into the sea. Now I am only wind, salt, and ruins. Who am I?
I am a bridge, but not an ordinary one. When ships pass underneath, I open like a gate. I connect the island of Rameswaram to the mainland. I am India's first sea bridge. Who am I?
Made of leather, came from the forest, announces the king's command to the town, calls warriors to battle. Its sound has been sung many times in Tamil literature. What is it?
She dances with a cone-shaped decorated pot balanced on her head, never letting it fall. This dance is performed at Amman temple festivals, especially in the month of Aadi. What dance is this?

The name itself means beauty. Performed all night during temple festivals in Kongu Nadu and the southern districts. In old times only men danced it. Women joined only in recent times. The beauty rests entirely in the movement of hands, feet, and body. What dance is this?

No mridangam, no thavil, no instrument at all. Standing in a circle, the sound of clapping hands alone is the rhythm. Women gather, sing, and keep the beat. Work, celebration, and community memory all meet here. What dance is this?
